5fcfa29a6f.why: Old clarity problem fixed: the 'counted up from the plants' instruction is cut, so 'Quaternary' is now only the count-the-seeds slip. NatGeo gives this very desert chain (mouse eats seeds, snake eats mouse, owl preys on snake) and puts tertiary consumers at the fourth level. Placing a chain's members on the numbered levels is 7th grade; T1 names only herbivore, carnivore and omnivore.

5ba2ee766f.why: Old tell fixed: the stem names the rule of thumb but no longer gives it, so the student must know the tenth and apply it twice. A tenth of a tenth is easy in the head. The wrong choices are the one-step slip (a tenth), three steps (a thousandth) and the adding slip (a fifth). HHMI gives about 10%, varying from 5 to 20%, which matches the context.

736100af8a.why: Fact-check points fixed: the stem now says 'rarely more than four or five' (Grokipedia: limits chains to about 4-5 levels), and the context names habitat size instead of productivity, which Post, Pace and Hairston support (big lakes have longer chains than small lakes of the same productivity). The key is no longer the longest choice. 'Destroys' (energy conservation), 'atoms used up' (matter cycles) and 'top predators hold most' (M2) are honest wrong choices.

44568db950.why: Old T1 tell fixed: 'make their own food' and 'take in no energy' are gone. Now 'every level' is set against 'only dead leaves and wood', and the two energy choices are live (T1's card says a log gives young trees no energy, which makes 'pass no energy on' tempting). Facts: decomposers are generally not given a fixed trophic level because they work across levels (Grokipedia); soil protists, nematodes and springtails eat bacteria and fungi, so 'pass no energy on' is false; on land most plant growth is not eaten while alive. 'They' is plural throughout.

f5ada8e3b6.why: Old grade problem fixed: the question now makes the student weigh many tiny grasshoppers against fewer, heavier songbirds (M5), with the energy-builds-up misconception (M2) as a wrong choice. Land biomass pyramids are upright (Grokipedia; NatGeo: biomass decreases with each level). Field figures agree: 40 years at the National Bison Range put grasshopper biomass at about 5 g per square metre (about 50 kg a hectare), twice that of the mammal herbivores, far above any songbird level. No number is in the choices; they are parallel and of even length.
